releases.body:
## What you can do now

- **Use merged project memories automatically without pulling or disturbing local work.** The plugin refreshes project memories in its own isolated checkout from the repository's remote default branch, leaving your current branch, staged files, and uncommitted edits untouched.
- **Receive merged global memories automatically.** When your global memory clone is on its default branch with no local edits to tracked files, the plugin fast-forwards it from the remote default branch automatically.
- **Carry pending project proposals across the upgrade automatically.** Existing local project proposals and audit state are copied once into the isolated project store on first use.

## Upgrading

No action is needed. Existing data and workflows continue to work.

## Known limitations

- The memory files visible inside your own project working copy still update only when you run a normal `git pull`.
- Global memory automatic refresh is skipped while your global clone is offline, on a non-default branch, or has local edits to tracked files.
- Legacy single-file `MEMORY.md` entries in Git repositories are left untouched rather than imported automatically as active memories.

## What you can do now

- **Carry knowledge everywhere, and keep repository rules in place.** One private global store reaches every session; each repository keeps its own store for rules that only make sense there. A proposal names its store (global by default once its clone exists), reads and reviews cover both, and the prompt shows one section per store.
- **Keep the two indexes in proportion.** The sections share one size limit, the global side is capped at a configurable share, and budget one side does not need is available to the other — a large global store cannot push project entries out.
- **Publish both stores at once, and never let one block the other.** Every store with pending proposals gets its own pull request; a failure in one never blocks the other, and a missing global clone degrades to project-only memory with one path-free line instead of an error.
- **Store only what the code cannot say.** The agent now asks whether the code, tests or design doc will state a rule once it is finished — skipping both "already implemented" and "not built yet" — and retires a memory with `implemented` when the artifact takes over, marked as graduated in its pull request.
- **Keep publishing out of your working tree.** The bot runs in a temporary worktree, removes only worktrees it can prove it created, honours a refusal from Git, and a leftover from an earlier crash no longer blocks later attempts.
- **Keep a bad state from breaking the session.** Unreadable entries are counted and omitted from the index instead of removing it, and a failing audit can no longer end a session with an error.

## Upgrading

No action is needed. Your existing memories stay where they are and keep working.

- **Set up a personal store only if you want one.** Create a private repository, copy it to the place the plugin looks for it, and give it the three folders the user guide describes. The next session finds it without a restart.
- **Prefer the old behaviour?** Leave the personal store unset and nothing changes, or turn it off explicitly in your settings.
- **Everything else already has a default.** The user guide lists the new settings, if you want to change how they behave.

## Known limitations

- Nothing is removed automatically, even when a finished feature makes a memory redundant. Removing one still takes a merged pull request.
- The background check reads memories in several passes, so it can miss a contradiction between two it never sees side by side.
- A merged memory appears in a session only after you pull it, and your personal store and each repository update separately.
- Not every memory is listed in every session. The index keeps to a fixed size and says when it is full, and the rest is one read away; raising the size limit lists more.

## What you can do now

- **Run the background memory audit with your own provider key.** On OpenCode 2.x the audit previously failed outright; it can now call an OpenAI-compatible provider directly, with a key you supply.
- **Keep audit work off your coding quota.** The audit can use a cheaper model, or a separate account, from the one you code with.

## Why this was needed

OpenCode 2.x relays model calls through its own inference gateway, and that gateway rejects an account credential — a personal access token or an OAuth login. The audit inherited that credential, so on 2.x it could fail with `HTTP 400 … Personal Access Tokens are not supported for this endpoint`.

That is a credential-type rejection, not a quota problem, and no amount of retrying fixes it. Audits that silently stopped running were the visible symptom.

## Setup

```jsonc
"auditProvider": {
  "baseUrl": "https://api.deepseek.com",
  "apiKey": "{file:~/.secrets/opencode/deepseek-api-key}",
  "model": "deepseek-flash"
  // "headers": { ... }   // optional, for endpoints needing more than a bearer token
}
```

- `apiKey` may be a literal, `{file:path}`, or `{env:NAME}`. A leading `~` is expanded.
- `baseUrl` may or may not already end in `/chat/completions`.

## Upgrading

- **If your audits already work, do nothing.** The option is opt-in.
- **If audits fail on OpenCode 2.x** with the rejection above, add `auditProvider` to the plugin options and set the three fields.

## Known limitations

- The endpoint must be OpenAI-compatible (`/chat/completions`).
- A provider that is present but incomplete is treated as an error rather than falling back to the host credential. Quietly continuing would hide that the option did nothing.
- Large stores are audited in batches, with a small overlap between them. A pair of memories that lands in different batches can still be missed.
- Keys the plugin knows about are scrubbed from its logs and error messages. A proxy that echoes a key back on its own is outside that guarantee.

## Install

```bash
opencode plugin add @chncaesar/opencode-plugin-memory@latest   # OpenCode 2.x
npm i @chncaesar/opencode-plugin-memory@0.6.0                  # manual
```

Full changelog: https://github.com/chncaesar/opencode-plugin-memory/compare/v0.5.0...v0.6.0

## What's new in v0.5.0

A small release with one idea behind it: **stop committing anything derived.**

### The index file is gone

Until now, `memory/_summary.md` was a committed index that CI regenerated on merge, and the injected prompt was built from it. That gave the store a second source of truth, and a workflow whose only job was keeping it in sync.

Both are deleted. Every session now derives the index directly from `memory/active/` at start:

```
[mem-D2oToptx] WebFetch 必须走 subagent，避免 context 膨胀
[mem-KP221qb2] OpenCode 2.x calls models through opencode.ai/inference…
```

Titles and IDs only, never bodies. Nothing is written to disk, so running OpenCode in a directory still does not create or modify a `memory/` folder there — and the index can no longer drift from what was merged, because it is computed from what was merged.

Consequences:

- The GitHub Actions workflow that regenerated the index is removed, along with the `[skip ci]` commit dance.
- `opencode-memory-bot regenerate` is kept as a **no-op** that prints an explanation, so older CI jobs that still call it fail nothing.
- Migration no longer writes an index at the end.

### The context budget is explicit

Only the index enters the system prompt, capped by `maxSummaryChars`. When the cap is hit, the model gets a subset plus a notice saying so, and can call `memory_read` for a specific body or `memory_review` to list the store. A growing store costs a growing index and nothing else.

### Housekeeping

- The committed `package-lock.json` is dropped from the repository.
- `AGENTS.md` and `DESIGN.md` updated for the derived index; the bot no longer knows about a summary file at all.

**Full changelog:** https://github.com/chncaesar/opencode-plugin-memory/compare/v0.4.0...v0.5.0

## What's new in v0.4.0

### The model can publish its own proposals

`memory_publish` is a sixth tool: argument-less, and it runs the bot itself, so proposals no longer sit in staging waiting for someone to remember the CLI.

It needs no user confirmation because it only opens PRs — the merge is the gate — and all git work happens in a throwaway `git worktree`, so your checkout, branch and uncommitted files are never touched. Leftover worktrees from a crashed run are cleaned up on the next one. A lock file (`.memory/bot.lock`, atomic, with stale-lock recovery) keeps a `watch` daemon and `memory_publish` from running at the same time; when the lock is held, the call reports it and processes nothing.

To make that reachable, the system prompt now carries a one-line notice when proposals are pending, telling the model to publish. Same division of labour as everywhere else: the model publishes, the human merges.

### The bot survives interruptions

Each run reports four counters — **promoted**, **recovered**, **skipped**, **failed**:

- **recovered** — the branch was already on the remote (an earlier run pushed it and stopped before the PR). The bot finds that PR, or opens it, and clears the staged file. No second commit, no duplicate branch.
- **skipped** — nothing to do (target already retired, or a PR that cannot be opened); the staged file is left in place.
- **failed** — git or `gh` refused; the file stays for the next run.

Remote and default branch are now detected from `origin` (both `git@…` and `https://…` forms) instead of assuming `main`.

### The audit handles a store it cannot fit in one prompt

New `auditBatchChars` (default `400000`) caps how much memory text goes into one audit call. A larger store is split into batches, ordered so related entries land together and with a 3-entry overlap, and a memory is never cut in two. The default assumes a ~1M-token model at roughly one token per character (Chinese); lower it for a smaller context window.

An over-long prompt is now recognised as a context overflow and explained with a fix (lower `auditBatchChars`, or point the audit at a model with a bigger window) rather than surfacing as a raw provider error. `memory_review` also reports how the last audit went, including failures.

On OpenCode 2.x the audit call uses the host's stateless `experimental.generate.text` with an abort timeout, instead of depending on a session or agent existing.

### Everything else

- `maxSummaryChars` default raised from `2000` to `10000` — the index costs one line per memory, so a small store no longer truncates.
- `memory_propose` / `memory_update` / `memory_delete` now say plainly that a proposal is *staged only* and that no pull request exists until `memory_publish` runs.

**Full changelog:** https://github.com/chncaesar/opencode-plugin-memory/compare/v0.3.0...v0.4.0
